analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and surgical centers to publicly report and post prices for common services and drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2005, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee's health subcommittee, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital and outpatient surgical center to report to the Department of Health and Human Services how often they perform their 75 most common services and administer their 50 most common inpatient drugs, and what they charge for each. HHS would post that data online in a format that lets patients compare prices across hospitals, and hospitals would have to post notices about it at every admission desk. Hospitals that knowingly failed to report could face fines up to $10,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, especially those paying out of pocket or carrying high-deductible insurance, who could compare what different hospitals charge for the same surgery or drug before choosing where to get care. Employers and insurers shopping on behalf of workers would also gain a public benchmark, since hospital charges were typically secret and varied widely between facilities.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers would have to report the average and median charge for their most frequently performed services and drugs twice a year, and HHS would post the data online in a format designed for price comparison across facilities [S2][S3].
Each hospital would have to prominently post a notice at every admission site telling patients the price data is available on the HHS website [S2][S3].

The reported charges must reflect the amount charged before any adjustment for negotiated insurance rates, so patients would see the sticker price that un-insured and out-of-network patients actually face [S3].
Hospitals that knowingly fail to report or post notice could face civil fines of up to $10,000 per violation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers, which would bear the cost of collecting, classifying, and reporting pricing data twice a year, and which would lose some of the pricing opacity that lets identical procedures carry very different prices at different facilities.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires disclosure of list charges, not what insurers actually pay, and the bill's own text says it does not regulate or set hospital charges [S3]. Published sticker prices can differ sharply from negotiated rates, so patients with insurance might learn little about what they would actually owe.
Hospitals would face new paperwork and compliance costs to classify services, compute averages and medians, and file semiannual electronic reports [S3], a burden smaller facilities would feel most.
Penalties are capped at $10,000 per knowing violation [S3], a modest amount for a large hospital system, so enforcement pressure would be limited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real but partial: knowing a hospital's sticker price for a common surgery or drug is far more transparency than patients had in 2005, and it matters most for the uninsured and people with high deductibles. But because the bill discloses pre-negotiation charges and does not regulate the charges themselves, insured patients could still face confusing bills. The main cost falls on hospitals in compliance work, which is comparatively small for large systems.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, was sent to its health subcommittee the next day, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Lipinski, joined by Rep. Bob Inglis of South Carolina, introduced the bill on June 30, 2005 [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on July 1 to the Subcommittee on Health, which is where consideration would have begun [S1][S5].
No further action is recorded; the bill never advanced to a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers benefited from the bill's death, keeping their prices undisclosed to patients two more years. Patients gained nothing until transparency requirements arrived through other means many years later.

for.name: Rep. Daniel Lipinski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Hospital Price Reporting and Disclosure Act of 2005 on June 30, 2005.

for.name: Rep. Bob Inglis
for.what_they_did: Joined Lipinski in introducing the bill as an original cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never advanced the bill beyond its Subcommittee on Health referral; no markup, hearing, or floor action was scheduled during the rest of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start: a Democratic sponsor with a Republican original cosponsor, and 5 cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but it drew no recorded opposition because it never reached a vote.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to disclose what they charge for their most common services and drugs, exposing wide price variation between facilities and making it easier for patients to shop. The bill died in committee, so hospitals kept price secrecy.
Surgical centers would face the same semiannual reporting and posting requirements and the same fines for noncompliance as hospitals.
Public charge data would have given insurers and employers shopping on behalf of workers a benchmark for negotiating with hospitals.
